common_name: Orange Sovereign Amaryllis (Classic Vivid Orange Amaryllis)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Orange Sovereign is a long-established Dutch cultivar prized for its clean, saturated orange color, one of the truest and most vivid oranges in the amaryllis trade.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Orange Sovereign has remained a mainstay of the Dutch bulb trade for decades on the strength of its brilliant, unusually pure orange color, which reads as warmer and more saturated in the garden than most other orange-toned amaryllis cultivars. In zone 8-10 gardens it can stay in the ground year-round, naturalizing into a larger clump over successive seasons, and its foliage should be allowed to grow and die back naturally after bloom to recharge the bulb. It also forces reliably indoors as a holiday container amaryllis, with a third of the bulb left exposed above the potting mix.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Amaryllis

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Liberty is a classic solid-red cultivar valued for its deep, velvety red petals and clean, unmarked color.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Liberty produces large, richly saturated red flowers with a velvety sheen and no white markings, giving it a bolder, more solid presence than striped or bicolor amaryllis cultivars. In zone 8-10 gardens it can remain in the ground year-round, where it naturalizes and slowly builds into a fuller clump, and foliage should be left to die back naturally after flowering to feed the bulb. Liberty is also a dependable choice for forcing into bloom indoors over winter, planted with roughly a third of the bulb above the potting mix.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Amaryllis

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Hercules is known for producing some of the largest flowers of any red amaryllis cultivar, on tall, sturdy stalks.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Hercules is grown for its outsized, bright red blooms, among the largest-flowered of the solid red amaryllis cultivars, carried on thick stems strong enough to support their weight without staking. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground year-round to naturalize, and the foliage should be allowed to grow and die back on its own after bloom rather than being cut back early. It also performs well as a forced holiday container bulb, planted with about a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Amaryllis

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Bestseller is one of the most widely grown amaryllis cultivars, named for its long-running commercial popularity and prized for its rich raspberry-red flowers.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Bestseller produces large flowers in a deep raspberry-red with subtly darker veining radiating from the throat, a color that has kept it a top-selling amaryllis cultivar for many years running. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground year-round, naturalizing into a fuller clump over time, and the strap-like foliage should be allowed to die back naturally after bloom to recharge the bulb for the following season. It is also a reliable choice for forcing into bloom indoors as a classic winter container amaryllis.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Amaryllis

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; Desire bears warm, sunset-toned orange-red flowers with a deeper glow toward the throat.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. Desire's large flowers combine warm orange and red tones that deepen toward the throat, giving each bloom a glowing, sunset-like quality that sets it apart from cooler true-red or true-orange cultivars. In zone 8-10 gardens it can remain in the ground year-round and will naturalize into an increasingly full clump, with foliage left to die back naturally after flowering to recharge the bulb. Desire also forces well indoors as a winter container amaryllis, planted with roughly a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Amaryllis

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; La Paz bears white flowers boldly brushed with red picotee edges and a red flame down the center of each petal, giving a candy-striped effect.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. La Paz's white petals are edged in bold red and marked with a red central flame down each one, producing a crisp, candy-striped look that stands out among the more uniformly colored amaryllis cultivars. In zone 8-10 gardens it can be left in the ground year-round to naturalize, and the foliage should be allowed to grow and die back on its own after bloom rather than being removed early. It is also well suited to forcing indoors as a decorative holiday container bulb, planted with about a third of the bulb above the potting mix.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Amaryllis

common_name: White Christmas Amaryllis (Large-Flowered Pure White Amaryllis)

planting.note: Plant bulbs in spring with the neck at or just above soil surface; White Christmas is a classic large-flowered pure white cultivar long favored for holiday forcing.

directions: Plant bulbs in fertile, well-drained soil in partial shade to morning sun, with the neck of the bulb at or just above the soil surface. White Christmas produces broad, rounded, pure white flowers of substantial size, a clean unmarked white that has made it a longtime favorite for holiday displays distinct from smaller-flowered or greenish-throated white cultivars. In zone 8-10 gardens it can stay in the ground year-round, naturalizing into a larger clump over time, and its foliage should be left to die back naturally after bloom to recharge the bulb. White Christmas is especially popular forced into bloom indoors for the winter holidays, planted with roughly a third of the bulb exposed above the potting mix.
sources: University of Florida IFAS Extension — Amaryllis
